claims.text: The magnetic high-entropy alloy has a typical disordered, single-phase, homogeneous initial microstructure.
A single-step aging heat treatment can induce nanoscale precipitates in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The precipitates produced by aging will be uniformly distributed.
The heat treatment is constrained to induce precipitation without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Nanoscale precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Precipitate pinning increases the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
Increasing the energy barrier for domain-wall motion enhances coercivity.
The aged alloy will have a higher coercive field than a matched unaged alloy.
The as-cast or as-solutionized baseline is homogeneous and lacks significant precipitate-based microstructure.
The coercivity enhancement should hold during room-temperature or otherwise standard magnetic testing.
A sufficient precipitate volume and an optimal precipitate size are required for coercivity enhancement.
Whether precipitation occurs depends on alloy chemistry.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on aging temperature and time and on the resulting precipitate size and distribution.
TEM or SEM can be used to assess precipitate presence and dispersion, while hysteresis loops can be used to extract coercive field.
Failure of aged samples to show a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to the control is specified as a falsifying result.
Failure to confirm uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that unsuitable aging parameters may fail to produce precipitates and therefore may yield no coercivity enhancement, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to form the precipitates as falsification. Failure to realize the stipulated mediator is an intervention-implementation failure rather than a decisive test of the proposed precipitate-to-coercivity mechanism.
